name: Brunei

most.note: Recommended for most people going to Brunei who haven't had it before. It spreads through food and water, and a good hotel doesn't remove the risk.
Check when you last had a tetanus, diphtheria and polio booster. If it was more than ten years ago and you'll be anywhere medical care is limited, a booster is recommended.
Spread through food and water. Recommended for most trips to Brunei, and especially if you're staying with family or eating away from the tourist trail.

some.note: Spread by daytime-biting mosquitoes, and bite avoidance is the main protection. Ask about the vaccine if you've had dengue before.
Worth considering for longer stays, for anyone who might need medical or dental treatment there, and for work with blood or needles.
Worth considering for rural stays of a month or more, or shorter stays in the transmission season near rice fields or pig farms.
Worth considering if you'll be around animals, in rural areas or far from medical care, and for children, who are bitten more often. The course takes three or four weeks, so book early.
Only for a few people: under-16s staying three months or more with local people, and healthcare workers.

certificates: A yellow fever certificate is asked for from travellers aged 9 months and over arriving from a country with yellow fever risk, or after more than 12 hours in transit through one. Flying straight from the UK, you won't need one.
Proof of polio vaccination may be asked for from some travellers.

malaria.line: There's a low malaria risk in parts of Brunei. Bite avoidance is the usual advice rather than tablets.
